units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: Write a group of answers to one question and let them set their own bar, so no second scoring network, the critic, is needed.

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: This page builds on RL Basics and Aligning Language Models with RL.

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: 1. An agent is the learner that picks the moves. A state is the agent's situation right now; a move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state; a reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad.

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: 2. A token is a word or a piece of a word; a language model writes its reply one token at a time.

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: 3. Here the agent is the language model. Here the state is the prompt plus the tokens written so far, and the move is the next token. Here the reward is one number for the whole reply, given when the reply ends.

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: 4. RL, short for reinforcement learning, is learning which moves to make from rewards rather than from labelled answers.

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: 5. A policy is the agent's rule for choosing a move in each state; it may always pick the same move or pick by chance. The policy is the language model being trained to write replies.

sections.section: 1 The critic is as big as the model

units.section: 1 The critic is as big as the model
units.spoken: Section one, The critic is as big as the model

units.section: 1 The critic is as big as the model
units.spoken: The critic is as big as the model

units.section: 1 The critic is as big as the model
units.spoken: What. Training a language model with RL needs a second network, a critic, about the same size as the model, and that critic is the cost GRPO removes.

units.section: 1 The critic is as big as the model
units.spoken: How. The critic guesses how the whole answer will be rewarded, at every point while it is written.

units.section: 1 The critic is as big as the model
units.spoken: Why. When it works, the policy learns without a second network to train, so the training run is smaller and cheaper.

units.section: 1 The critic is as big as the model
units.spoken: The usual way to train a language model with reinforcement learning needs that second network, which adds a whole second model to train and a large memory and compute cost.

units.section: 1 The critic is as big as the model
units.spoken: The critic has to guess, at every point while the answer is written, how the whole answer will be rewarded, though the reward arrives only once at the end, so its guesses are hard to make accurate.

units.section: 1 The critic is as big as the model
units.spoken: Its guess is the score the answer can be expected to get, on average over the ways it could turn out, and each answer is compared with it so the update knows which tokens to push up and which down, where pushing up means raising the chance the model gives that answer.

units.section: 1 The critic is as big as the model
units.spoken: The running example is a grade-school math question with one known final answer, and the competition is between the model's own answers to it, not between students or models. The model writes its reasoning and then its final answer, and a program checks whether that answer matches the known one.

units.section: 1 The critic is as big as the model
units.spoken: Take a look at this figure. One question, one answer, and the final answer in a box. The baker question sits on top: five trays of twelve muffins, forty-seven sold in the morning, two more trays baked, half of those sold. The model's answer shows its reasoning first, then its final answer in a box, marked right when it matches the known one. The lesson is the setup: one question, one answer, and a checker that marks it right or wrong.

units.section: 1 The critic is as big as the model
units.spoken: The question is one in the style of the grade-school math questions in GSM8K, a set of grade-school math word problems with known answers: a baker makes 5 trays of 12 muffins and sells 47 in the morning. Then she bakes 2 more trays and sells half of those. How many muffins are left? It is made here to show the method, not a GSM8K item, and its arithmetic is not worked on this page.

sections.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: Section two, Let the other answers set the bar

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: Let the other answers set the bar

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: What. For one question, the policy writes several answers, and their average reward is the bar, the score an answer can be expected to get. That bar, expected score, baseline and group average are four names for one thing.

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: How. Each answer's reward is compared with that bar, not with a score from a critic.

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: Why. When it works, an answer that beat its group is pushed up and one below it is pushed down, so the model learns from its own spread.

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: 2.1One reward per answer

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: The group is the answers to the muffin question, each marked right or wrong by a checker, a program that checks the final answer, or by a reward model, a network trained to score answers from solutions that were checked automatically. The muffin question uses a checker, and the runs behind GRPO score with a reward model.

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: For a math question, the model writes an answer and gets one reward for it.

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: With a right answer rewarded one and a wrong one zero, the raw reward would never push a wrong answer down and would push every right answer by the same amount.

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: 2.2The push needs a bar to compare against

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: The policy gradient pushes each move the agent played by a score of how well it turned out, up when the score is positive and down when it is negative.

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: The return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less.

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: Here the reward arrives when the reply ends and later rewards are not counted any less, so the return from any point in a reply is the reward the finished reply gets.

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: An expected value is the average over everything that can happen by chance, weighted by how likely each outcome is.

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: PPO, proximal policy optimization, is the usual RL method for language models.

units.section: 2 Let the other answers set the bar
units.spoken: Take a look at this figure. Two columns, PPO on the left and GRPO on the right, doing the same job with one part swapped. On the PPO side, the policy writes the answers, the reference stays frozen, the reward model scores each answer, and the critic guesses the expected score, and the advantage is built from the critic's guesses and the real rewards. On the GRPO side, the policy writes a group of K answers, the reward model scores them, and the group average is the expected score, and the advantages come straight from the group average, one per answer. The lesson is the swap: the group replaces the critic.

sections.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Section three, How the group comparison becomes an update

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: With the critic gone, the group has to do its job inside the update itself: the group average sets the bar, the ratio says how far each token has moved, and the update stays small and close to where the model started.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: SFT, supervised fine-tuning, trains the model on replies people wrote with the ordinary next-token loss; RL usually starts from that model.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: DeepSeekMath is a language model trained to reason about math, and its starting policy, DeepSeekMath-Instruct, is such an SFT model.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: The reference model is a frozen copy of the SFT model.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: KL measures how different two probability distributions are, zero when they match; the KL penalty charges the policy for drifting away from the reference model.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: GRPO adds this penalty straight to its loss, not to each token's reward.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: 3.1Advantage from the group

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Advantage from the group

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: What. One answer's push is set by how it did against the other answers to the same question, not by a critic's guess.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: How. The advantage is the answer's reward minus the group mean, divided by the group standard deviation, and every token of one answer shares that answer's one push. This is outcome supervision: one reward per answer, shared by all its tokens.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Why. When it works, an answer that beat its group is pushed up as a whole, and one below it is pushed down.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Equation 1. The group advantage. Training a math model without a critic needs some other bar to score answers against, and the group itself can set it. A math tutor marking several answers to one question against each other, rather than against a grading rubric, faces the same job.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Take a look at this equation. The group itself can set the bar, so the group average scores the answers.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: The advantage line. A hat sub i is answer i's advantage, the push its tokens get. Ar sub i is answer i's reward. Mean is the group average, the K rewards added and divided by K. Std is the group spread, how far apart the group's scores are. K counts the answers per question. Above the mean, the top is positive and the answer is pushed up; below it, negative and pushed down. Intuitively, the advantage is the reward minus the group mean, over the group spread.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Intuition. Without a critic, the group itself has to supply the expected score, and the average of its rewards does that job.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Example. An answer matching the known final answer sits above the average and is pushed up, while one that misses sits below and is pushed down.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: The token line. A hat sub i tee is the advantage of token tee of answer i. A hat sub i is the answer's one advantage. Tee runs from one through the length of why sub i, so it covers every token. Why sub i is answer i, and the bars read its length in tokens. Intuitively, every token of one answer shares that answer's one push.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Intuition. Every token of one answer shares that answer's one push, so one group score moves the whole answer.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Example. One muffin answer: its first token and its last token carry the same advantage, so the whole answer rises or falls together.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: So each answer is scored by how far its reward sits from its group's average, measured against how far apart the group's rewards are, and every token shares that one score.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: With the muffin question and its group of answers, when every answer in the group agrees, the average equals every reward and no token is pushed either way.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: 3.2How far each token has moved

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: How far each token has moved

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: What. The ratio says how far a token has moved since the answers were written: the chance now, over the chance then.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: How. Each token gets its own ratio, the current chance over the old chance, so a token the policy now favors has a ratio above one.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Why. When it works, a ratio of one means the push equals the advantage, so a fresh batch teaches at full strength. The same idea works at the answer level: one ratio per whole answer instead of one per token, the chance the policy gives the whole answer now over the chance the old policy gave it.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Here a batch is a set of prompts and the replies the policy just wrote for them, trained on together.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: The old policy is the policy as it was when it wrote these replies.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Equation 2. The token ratio. Each update reuses the answers the old policy wrote, so training needs a number that says how far each token's chance has already moved since those answers were written. A teacher who re-grades the same homework after a lesson wants to know how much each grade has moved since the first grading.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Take a look at this equation. Each update reuses the answers the old policy wrote, so training needs a number that says how far each token has already moved.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: The ratio line. Rho sub i tee is the ratio for token tee of answer i, a function of the weights thay-ta. Pee sub thay-ta is the policy now, and its chance of writing that token, why sub i tee, given the question ex and the tokens before it, why sub i less than tee, is the top. Pee sub thay-ta old is the old policy, the frozen snapshot that wrote the answers. Above one, the token has become more likely; below one, less likely; at one, unchanged. Intuitively, the ratio is the chance now over the chance then, for one token.
termList: why sub i less than tee

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Intuition. Training must know how far each token's chance moved, the same check PPO makes.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Example. The token in a muffin answer that writes the number of muffins left: if training has made it more likely, its ratio sits above one.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: So the ratio is the chance now over the chance then, and when it sits at one the push equals the advantage.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: 3.3Keeping the update small and close

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Keeping the update small and close

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: What. The objective is one line per token: the ratio times the advantage, clipped inside a band, averaged over the group and over each answer's tokens, minus a price for drifting from the reference.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: How. The min takes the smaller of the unclipped push and the clipped push, so a token that already moved past the edge earns no extra push, and the KL term subtracts the drift price.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Why. When it works, a batch reused for several updates cannot move the model far, and the policy stays near the reference model.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Clipping holds the ratio between two clip edges, so an update stops rewarding a helpful change once it passes an edge.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: A gradient tells training how to change the weights, and how far, and a token's log-chance is the log of the chance the model gives that token.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Equation 3. The GRPO objective. Without a critic, the group comparison has to do the critic's job inside the update itself, while the update still stays small and stays close to where the model started. A coach who scores players against each other, pushes the good plays, and keeps the team playing its own game does all three at once.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Take a look at this equation. The group comparison has to do the critic's job inside the update itself, while the update still stays small and stays close to where the model started.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: The objective line. J sub gee ar pee oh is the objective, a function of the weights thay-ta. E is the expected value, the average over what chance draws. Ex is one of the batch's math questions, drawn from the question distribution pee of cue. Why sub i is the group of answers the old policy wrote, drawn at random from the old policy pee sub thay-ta old. Intuitively, the objective is the expected value, over questions and the groups written for them, of the big bracket that follows.
termList: J sub gee ar pee oh

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Intuition. The objective is an average over questions and the answers written for them, with the group comparison doing the critic's job inside it.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Example. The muffin question: it enters the average with the group the old policy wrote for it.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: The averages line. One over K times the sum over i from one to K averages over the group's answers. One over the length of why sub i times the sum over tee from one to the length of why sub i averages over the tokens of answer i. K counts the answers per question, and tee counts the tokens of one answer. Intuitively, the line first averages over each answer's tokens, then over the group's answers.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Intuition. Two averages sit inside each other: over each answer's tokens first, then over the group's answers.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Example. One muffin answer with more tokens than another: its tokens are averaged first, so the longer answer counts no more than the shorter one in the group average.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: The push line. Min takes the smaller of the two terms, and the big round bracket opens the first term. Rho sub i tee times A hat sub i tee is the token's ratio times its advantage. Maximizing this product raises the chance of tokens in answers with a positive advantage, and lowers it for tokens in answers with a negative one. Intuitively, the push for one token is the smaller of two versions of the same product, the ratio times the advantage.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Intuition. The push for one token is the smaller of two versions of the same product, the ratio times the advantage.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Example. One token of a muffin answer that matched the known final answer: its advantage is positive, so the product pushes its chance up.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: The clip line. Clip holds the ratio inside a band, keeping rho sub i tee between one minus epsilon sub clip and one plus it. Epsilon sub clip is the clip size, PPO's clip hyper-parameter. The clipped ratio is then multiplied by the token's advantage, A hat sub i tee. Intuitively, a token whose ratio already moved past the edge in the direction of its push earns no extra push.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Intuition. The clip holds the ratio inside a band, so a reused batch cannot move the model far, the same guard PPO uses.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Example. One token while DeepSeekMath trains: the ratio sits at one, so the push equals the advantage, and the token is pushed by its advantage times the gradient of its log-chance.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: The KL line. The minus sign subtracts the price of drifting. Beta is the KL penalty strength. K L sub tee is the single-sample estimate of the drift, never negative, zero when the two agree. The double bar separates the policy pee sub thay-ta from the reference pee sub ref. Intuitively, the line subtracts beta times the drift, so the KL sits in the objective directly, not folded into the reward.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Intuition. Drifting from the starting model costs, and beta sets the price, charged here as its own term, not inside the reward.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Example. One muffin token: its KL charge pulls it back toward the reference, so chasing reward cannot drag the wording into odd text.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: So the objective averages the smaller of the two pushes over the group's tokens, minus beta times the drift, so the update improves the answers without letting the model drift into odd text.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: With the muffin question and its group of answers, the answers that match the known final answer earn a push up on every token, the ones that miss are pushed down, the clip stops any token from moving far in one update, and the KL term keeps the wording close to the starting model, so the update improves the answers without letting the model drift into odd text.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: 3.4PPO and GRPO side by side

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: This table lines up PPO and GRPO side by side across six rows. Read across a row to see one difference, and down the columns to see each method whole. Where the expected score comes from: PPO trains a critic network alongside the policy, while GRPO takes the average reward of the K answers to the same question. Advantage: PPO gives one per token, from the critic's guesses, while GRPO gives one per answer, shared by all its tokens. Where the KL penalty sits: in RLHF, each token's reward carries a small KL charge, so the KL changes the advantage, while GRPO puts a separate term in the objective, the KL term subtracted after the clipped push, so it leaves the advantage alone. Networks trained: PPO trains the policy and the critic, while GRPO trains only the policy, though the reward model also trains in iterative GRPO, which works in rounds. Replies written per prompt: PPO usually writes one, while GRPO writes a group of K. What stays the same: the ratio, the clip and the smaller of the two pushes, the frozen reference, and the reward model or checker.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: 3.5Scoring the whole answer or each step

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Scoring the whole answer or each step

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: What. Process supervision rewards each step of an answer, not only the final answer, so a good ending built on wrong steps gets caught.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: How. A process reward model scores each step, a network trained on checked solutions. Math-Shepherd is one such model, trained to score each step of a math answer. Each step score is normalized by the mean and spread over all step scores of all answers, the pooled set, and each token's push is the sum of the normalized scores from its step onward.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Why. When it works, the model learns good steps, not only good endings, so its reasoning improves where outcome scores cannot see.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Take one muffin answer in three steps: the tokens in step 1 are pushed by the sum of all three normalized scores, the tokens in step 2 by the last two, and the tokens in step 3 by its own score alone.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Take a look at this figure. One answer to the muffin question split into three steps, each step scored, with longer bars for higher scores. The scores accumulate backward: the tokens in step one are credited with all three scores, the tokens in step two with the last two, and the tokens in step three with its own score alone. The lesson is the credit: each token is pushed by the scores from its step to the end.

units.section: 3 How the group comparison becomes an update
units.spoken: Two answers to the muffin question can both reach the right boxed answer, one by sound steps and one by a lucky route; outcome supervision cannot tell them apart, and only step scores separate them.

sections.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: Section four, One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: What. One iteration takes a batch of questions, writes a group of answers to each, scores them, and pushes the policy toward the answers that beat their group.

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: How. The old policy writes the answers, the reward model or checker scores them, the group average sets the bar, and the clipped update pushes the tokens.

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: Why. When it works, the reference resets so the drift price always measures against a recent model, and the reward model keeps training so its scores stay honest as the policy improves.

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: 4.1What runs and how often

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: Each iteration runs the policy, which trains, and the reference, which stays frozen, plus the reward model or the checker. Each question gets K answers per iteration, and one iteration costs writing K answers for each question in the batch, so a bigger K or a bigger batch costs more.

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: Iterative GRPO works in rounds. Each round runs M batches, and within each batch the policy updates mu times; DeepSeekMath's runs use mu equals 1, one update per batch, and ran two rounds, the first giving the biggest gain. After each round the reference is reset to the current policy, and the reward model keeps training on fresh policy samples with a tenth of older data kept.

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: Intuition. One iteration is eight moves: take a batch and copy the policy as the old policy, write answers, score them, set the bar, take the advantage per answer, take the ratio for each token, push each token, and move on.

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: The mathematics. The advantage step turns each reward into a push against the group mean and spread, the ratio step compares each token's chance now with its chance then, and the update step takes the smaller of the two pushes and subtracts the price of drifting from the reference.

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: Example. The muffin question rides along: the old policy writes its answers, the checker marks them, and the tokens of the answers that beat the group average are pushed up.

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: Take a look at this walkthrough. It runs one GRPO iteration on a batch of questions, step by step: take a batch and copy the policy as the old policy, write K answers, score them, take the group average and spread, take the advantage per answer, take the ratio for each token, push each token with the clipped update and the KL penalty, then move on to the next batch. The lesson is the order: the batch becomes answers, the answers become scores, and the scores become the push.

units.spoken: The clipped push holds the ratio inside its band.

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: The KL step. Beta times K L sub tee subtracts the price of drifting from the reference pee sub ref. Beta is the KL penalty strength, and K L sub tee is the drift estimate. Intuitively, the KL term subtracts the price of drifting from the reference.

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: The KL term subtracts the price of drifting from the reference.

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: So one iteration writes a group of answers, scores them against their own average, and pushes each token by its answer's score while the KL term holds the wording near the starting model.

units.section: 4 One GRPO iteration on a batch of questions
units.spoken: One batch holds the muffin question. The old policy writes its answers, the checker marks them, the group average sets the bar, and every token is pushed by its answer's score while the KL term holds the wording near the starting model, so one iteration moves the model a small step toward answers that match the known one.

sections.section: 5 Group advantages and the GRPO loss

units.section: 5 Group advantages and the GRPO loss
units.spoken: Section five, Group advantages and the GRPO loss

units.section: 5 Group advantages and the GRPO loss
units.spoken: The code keeps the same four pieces PPO uses: the token log-probabilities, the old policy's log-probabilities, the reference log-probabilities, and the advantage per answer. The log-probabilities are shaped (num_answers, length), answers by tokens, with a mask for padding, blank filler tokens added so every answer in the batch has the same length; the mask zeroes the padding tokens, so they contribute nothing. The function returns the negative of J, so minimizing it maximizes J. logp_old and logp_ref come from frozen models and are computed without gradients; only logp carries the policy's gradient. The ratio in the code is the token ratio, and at one the push equals the advantage. The 0.2 clip edge is PPO's value, and the 0.04 KL strength is DeepSeekMath's.

units.section: 5 Group advantages and the GRPO loss
units.spoken: The code below computes the muffin question's group advantages and loss: the reward row is the group's marks, right or wrong, and the log-probability rows are the policy's chances for each answer's tokens.

units.section: 5 Group advantages and the GRPO loss
units.spoken: This code is the GRPO loss in PyTorch, in two parts. The first part defines the group advantage: it takes the reward row for a group of answers, subtracts the group mean, and divides by the group spread, with a small guard that stops the division when the spread is zero. The second part defines the loss: it takes each answer's token log-probabilities from the policy, the old policy and the reference, plus the advantage per answer and a mask for padding. It builds the token ratio from the difference of log chances, takes the smaller of the unclipped push and the clipped push, subtracts beta times the KL estimate, masks the padding, averages over each answer's tokens and then over the group, and returns the negative of that average, so minimizing it maximizes the objective. The five notes below walk through each numbered piece in order.

units.section: 5 Group advantages and the GRPO loss
units.spoken: 1. The group advantage: the reward minus the group mean, over the group spread. An all-equal group gives a zero spread, and the guard, added beyond the equation, stops the division by that zero spread.

units.section: 5 Group advantages and the GRPO loss
units.spoken: 2. The token ratio: exp of the difference of log chances is the current chance over the old chance, per token.

units.section: 5 Group advantages and the GRPO loss
units.spoken: 3. The clipped push: the smaller of the ratio times the advantage and the clipped ratio times the advantage.

units.section: 5 Group advantages and the GRPO loss
units.spoken: 4. The single-sample KL estimate, DeepSeekMath equation 4: the reference chance over the policy chance, minus the log of that ratio, minus one.

units.section: 5 Group advantages and the GRPO loss
units.spoken: 5. The average over each answer's tokens, then over the group.

units.section: 6 The group is the baseline
units.spoken: Section six, The group is the baseline

units.section: 6 The group is the baseline
units.spoken: Intuition. The group average is the bar, and each answer is pushed by how far it sits from that bar.

units.section: 6 The group is the baseline
units.spoken: The mathematics. Each answer's push is its reward minus the group mean, over the group spread. Larger groups hold steadier advantages, because more answers make the average less noisy. When every answer scores the same, the spread is zero and nothing is pushed.

units.section: 6 The group is the baseline
units.spoken: Example. The closer a group splits evenly, the harder it pushes: the answers sit far from the average, so each push is large. With eight muffin answers, five right and three wrong, the five rise, the three fall, and the group pushes 7.7 in total, the sizes of the eight pushes added together.

units.section: 6 The group is the baseline
units.spoken: Take a look at this tool. The arrows show each answer's push from the group average: right answers sit above the line and are pushed up, wrong ones below it and pushed down. Two knobs change the picture: group size K, from small to large, and question difficulty, from easy to hard. The lesson is the spread: a group that splits evenly pushes hardest, and a uniform group teaches nothing.

units.section: 6 The group is the baseline
units.spoken: Try the tool. Move the group size knob from small to large and watch the arrows steady as the average gets less noisy. Move the difficulty knob from easy to hard and watch the group split change. When every answer scores the same, the arrows vanish, because a uniform group teaches nothing.

units.section: 6 The group is the baseline
units.spoken: Each new group is drawn from the same model; nothing is trained here.

units.section: 6 The group is the baseline
units.spoken: The run draws group after group, then stops.

sections.section: 7 GRPO next to other ways of training on rewarded answers

units.section: 7 GRPO next to other ways of training on rewarded answers
units.spoken: Section seven, GRPO next to other ways of training on rewarded answers

units.section: 7 GRPO next to other ways of training on rewarded answers
units.spoken: Rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) writes answers with the fixed SFT model, keeps the right ones and fine-tunes on them. It fits when answers can be checked and the model only needs to learn from its own correct answers.

units.section: 7 GRPO next to other ways of training on rewarded answers
units.spoken: Online RFT does the same with answers from the current model as it trains, sampling fresh answers and keeping the correct ones. It beats GRPO when every answer in a group is right, since GRPO's group advantage is then zero, while Online RFT still trains on the correct answers.

units.section: 7 GRPO next to other ways of training on rewarded answers
units.spoken: On the muffin question, GRPO pushes wrong answers down and sizes each push by the advantage, which is why it beats online RFT: online RFT only pushes right answers up.

units.section: 7 GRPO next to other ways of training on rewarded answers
units.spoken: DPO, direct preference optimization, trains on fixed preference pairs, built by a program checking which answer was right, with one loss and no reward model. It fits when pairs of good and bad answers are available and no reward model is wanted.

units.section: 7 GRPO next to other ways of training on rewarded answers
units.spoken: This table lines up five ways of training on rewarded answers across four columns: where the answers come from, what decides the reward, where the expected score comes from, and how strongly each answer is pushed. Read across a row to see one method, and down a column to compare them all. SFT uses fixed data, a person's label, no expected score, and pushes every answer equally. RFT uses the fixed SFT model, a program that checks the answer, no expected score, and pushes equally. Online RFT uses the current model, a program that checks the answer, no expected score, and pushes equally. DPO uses fixed data, a program's check used to build the pairs, no expected score, and pushes by how wrong the ranking still is. GRPO uses the current model, a reward model or a checker, the group average, and pushes by its advantage. The lesson is the last column: only GRPO sizes each push by how the answer did against its group.

units.section: 8 Settings for a GRPO run
units.spoken: Section eight, Settings for a GRPO run

units.section: 8 Settings for a GRPO run
units.spoken: TRL, Hugging Face's open library for training language models with these methods, has a GRPOTrainer. Its defaults have changed between releases, so set the KL weight (beta), the reward normalization (scale_rewards) and the loss type (loss_type) explicitly and check the GRPOConfig docs for the version you install. Reward normalization divides each group's rewards by their spread, and the loss type picks which variant's loss to use.

units.section: 8 Settings for a GRPO run
units.spoken: The learning rate eta sets how big a step each update takes.

units.section: 8 Settings for a GRPO run
units.spoken: This table lists the eight settings that shape a GRPO run and what each one does when it moves. Read across a row to see one setting, its value, and what raising or lowering it does. Group size K is 64 answers per question: raise it for steadier advantages and more compute, lower it for noisier and cheaper. Max answer length is 1,024 tokens: raise it for longer reasoning allowed, lower it for truncated answers. Batch is 1,024 questions: raise it for steadier, lower it for noisier. Policy learning rate eta is 1e-6: raise it for faster and less stable, lower it for slower. Reward-model learning rate is 2e-5: raise it for faster and less stable, lower it for slower. KL strength beta is 0.04: raise it to stay near the reference, lower it for freer drift. Clip epsilon clip is not stated in DeepSeekMath; epsilon is PPO's clip hyper-parameter, and the code uses 0.2, the value from the PPO paper: raise it for bigger steps, lower it for smaller steps. Policy updates per batch mu is 1: raise it for more reuse of each batch, lower it for one update per batch.

units.section: 8 Settings for a GRPO run
units.spoken: The clip only bites when a batch is reused for several updates. DeepSeekMath makes one update per sampled batch, so the clip never acts there, and more updates per batch would let it act, at a risk of drift.

sections.section: 9 When GRPO is the right tool

units.section: 9 When GRPO is the right tool
units.spoken: Section nine, When GRPO is the right tool

units.section: 9 When GRPO is the right tool
units.spoken: On-policy means learning from answers the same policy just wrote.

units.section: 9 When GRPO is the right tool
units.spoken: Policy gradients are on-policy, because each push counts a move as often as the current policy plays it, so play by an older or different policy would push by the wrong amounts.

units.section: 9 When GRPO is the right tool
units.spoken: GRPO is on-policy; it writes fresh answers every iteration.

units.section: 9 When GRPO is the right tool
units.spoken: GRPO fits when answers can be ranked for the same question, by a checker or by a reward model.

units.section: 9 When GRPO is the right tool
units.spoken: It fits when answers are long, where a per-token critic is hard to train.

units.section: 9 When GRPO is the right tool
units.spoken: It fits when memory is limited, where a second model of the same size does not fit.

units.section: 9 When GRPO is the right tool
units.spoken: Use DPO when you only have fixed pairs and no way to score new answers.

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: Section ten, How group advantages go wrong

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: Group-advantage failures and their fixes

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: What. Every failure in this section is one way the group advantage goes wrong: the group teaches nothing, the reward is gamed, the policy collapses, or the scores mislead.

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: How. Each failure has its own fix: widen the group or the question mix, check answers by rule where possible, hold the clip edges, and read the right score.

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: Why. When it works, the group keeps teaching because its answers still differ, the rewards still mean what they say, and the update still stays small.

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: In GRPO each answer's push depends on how far apart the group's scores are and on its length.

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: Entropy H is how undecided the policy is; it is high when the moves are about equally likely and zero when one move is certain.

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: Entropy collapse means the model's choices become nearly certain.

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: Then the answers in a group look alike and the model stops trying different answers.

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: Reward hacking is when the policy finds replies that score high without being good.

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: A checker that compares final answers is much harder to fool than a learned reward model.

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: Pass at n is the chance that at least one of n sampled answers is right.

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: Maj at n is the accuracy of the most common answer among n samples.

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: DAPO bundles four fixes for the failures below. It drops groups where every answer scores the same, so only mixed groups train. For answers that stop varying, it clips with two edges, 0.2 below and 0.28 above, so rarely chosen tokens can still gain probability. It averages over all tokens in the group instead of per answer. For overlong answers, Soft Overlong Punishment adds a length penalty, 0 down to -1, to the rule reward, a reward a program gives by checking the answer against a rule, worth +1 for a match and -1 otherwise. Overlong Filtering masks answers cut off by the length limit out of the loss, so a sound chain is not punished only for its length. Use DAPO when a run wastes groups or lets long answers grow: on the muffin question it keeps the mixed groups and cuts the padded ones.

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: Dr. GRPO removes two divisions: the standard-deviation division and the length division. Without the spread division, a group whose answers nearly all agree no longer counts for more than its small differences deserve. Under the length division, each answer counts the same in total, so a long wrong answer's tokens each count less and long wrong answers grow; without it, every token counts the same. Use Dr. GRPO when long answers or near-unanimous groups skew the update, as with a long wrong muffin answer.

units.section: 10 How group advantages go wrong
units.spoken: This table lines up what breaks GRPO, what it looks like, and the fix for each. Read across a row to see one cause, its symptom and its fix, and down the rows to compare the failures. When every answer in a group gets the same reward, the muffin question's group goes all right or all wrong, so the advantage is zero, nothing is pushed and the samples are wasted; the fix is to sample more questions and drop the all-same groups from the batch, as DAPO does, and mix difficulties. When the update divides by each answer's length, a long wrong muffin answer gets longer, more thinking that is just padding, because it shares its negative push among more tokens, so each token is punished less; the fix is that Dr. GRPO removes the length division, and DAPO averages over all tokens in the group instead. When the update divides by how far apart the group's scores are, the muffin question's group, when its answers earn almost the same reward, counts for more than its small differences deserve, because dividing by the spread scales those differences up; the fix is that Dr. GRPO removes this division too. When entropy collapses, the muffin question's answers become near identical, and the model stops trying different answers; the fix is that with several updates per batch, DAPO raises the upper clip edge only, so rarely chosen tokens can still gain probability and answers stay varied. When K is small, the muffin question's group average is noisy, so its advantages are noisy; the fix is a larger K, though the cost grows with K. When a reward model is hacked, the reward-model scores for the muffin question's answers rise while the answers get worse; the fix is rule checkers where possible. When RL sharpens rather than teaches, on GSM8K and MATH with DeepSeekMath 7B at temperature 0.7, Maj at n rises while Pass at n stays about flat, so RL makes the model pick its right answers more reliably but does not teach it to solve questions it could never solve; the fix is to train on prompts unlike the training ones, questions the model has not seen, and sample them with stronger search that hunts for the ones it cannot yet solve, the direction DeepSeekMath section 5.2.3 points to.

sections.section: 11 From math rewards to long reasoning

units.section: 11 From math rewards to long reasoning
units.spoken: Section eleven, From math rewards to long reasoning

units.section: 11 From math rewards to long reasoning
units.spoken: GRPO with rule rewards leads to longer reasoning. Long reasoning is a long chain of thought written before the final answer. Longer chains reach right answers more often, so the update keeps the longer successful chains.

units.section: 11 From math rewards to long reasoning
units.spoken: With rule rewards, the muffin question's successful chains grow longer. DeepSeek-R1-Zero is a reasoning model trained with reinforcement learning on math and code questions, starting from the DeepSeek-V3 base model, and its training run tracked answer length and accuracy as training went on. DeepSeek-R1-Zero shows length and accuracy growing together during training, which fits the idea that longer chains reach right answers more often, but the same growth has a competing reading: the Dr. GRPO length bias can stretch answers without making them better. That growth is reported in the DeepSeek-R1 paper, and DeepSeek-R1 is the later multi-stage model built on it.
